summary: Summation No. 22 covers non-military activities in Occupied Japan for July 1947, under the Katayama coalition Cabinet. Its centrepiece is the Economic Stabilization Board's first-ever "White Paper" (4 July), which reproduces in full the Government's account of deficits in state finance, industry and household budgets, exhausted stockpiles, inflation, falling labor productivity and the food and fuel crisis. Political coverage follows the proposed nationalization of coal mines, the Super-Emergency Food Program, civil-service reform demands, party realignment rumours, the Seko hoarded-materials scandal and further purge measures. Economic sections give June/May statistics for agriculture and land reform, coal, metals, chemicals, housing, textiles, power, communications, labor (union mergers, the 5 July standard-wage schedule, 12-percent coal wage rise), foreign trade resumption, rationing, finance, liquidation, antitrust (Fair Trade Commission) and property control. Social sections report typhus/DDT campaigns, repatriation, new education workshops and media activity. Historians will find dense monthly series and primary-source Japanese policy statements.
highlights: On 4 July the Economic Stabilization Board released Japan's first "White Paper" on the economy, citing exhausted stockpiles, inflation, delayed remedies and labor productivity below 40 percent of prewar, and warning of subsidy cuts, heavier taxes and cancelled ration days.

A June price stabilization program set official prices on cost of production, capping 13 key commodities at 65 times 1934-36 levels, backed by a 12-billion-yen subsidy fund and wages averaging 1,600 yen a month.

Local Land Commissions bought 536,745 acres of tenant land in July, 131,192 acres above plan, bringing land purchased for resale under the Land Reform Law to 853,506 acres of a 3,712,195-acre program.

Coal control dominated politics: a Social Democratic committee voted 3 July to nationalize mines, Democrats and Liberals resisted, and coal workers and operators agreed on 25 July to a 12-percent sliding-scale wage rise.
Liberal Diet member Koichi Seko charged that 50 billion yen of war materials were hoarded in hiding, and the House of Representatives appointed a 30-man investigating committee on 25 July.

Staple deliveries ran up to 21.6 days behind in major cities (Fukuoka), so the Cabinet approved a Super-Emergency Food Program on 23 July with fertilizer and silk bonuses for farmers delivering above 110-percent quotas; 41 percent of the July ration was imported.

The Fair Trade Commission was established 1 July and its seven commissioners appointed 14 July; 92 control companies were designated for liquidation, and Mitsui and Mitsubishi Trading Companies were ordered dissolved.
War crimes trials had tried 286 defendants by 24 July (276 convicted, 26 sentenced to death), and Japanese repatriation from 30 June to 27 July totaled 65,672, mostly from Soviet-controlled areas.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover for Summation No. 22 (July 1947), the table of contents for Parts I-IV, and the list of 114 charts, maps and graphs.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: no SCAP reorganization, the 4 July White Paper and coal-control politics, June production and labor items, finance, property control, and social, education and media activity.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: Reports no change in the organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during July.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: Covers the 4 July White Paper, coal-control disputes, civil-service demands, the 12-25 July Diet recess, Cabinet Order No. 119 on the purge, and 1,870 pending war-crimes investigations.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Digest of agriculture (853,506 acres of land bought), coal and oil, heavy industry, textiles, transport, the 12-percent coal wage rise, trade, rationing, finance and the new Fair Trade Commission.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: Digest of DDT dusting of 1,500,000 schoolchildren, 65,672 repatriates, the first education workshops, 1,213 foreign missionaries, women's broadcasts and SCAP Library attendance of 686 daily.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Politics dominated by the White Paper, coal control and the Seko case, followed by May-June public safety statistics, judicial administration and war-crimes processing.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Reproduces the 4 July White Paper, then covers coal nationalization, the 23 July Super-Emergency Food Program, party maneuvers, the Seko scandal, the purge, personnel changes and governors' autonomy complaint.

sections.title: Analysis of Japan's Economic Position and Text of the White Paper
sections.summary: Analysis and text of the White Paper: government, industry and household deficits, prices, wages, food, coal, power, transport, finance, labor and trade; cost of living cited at 60-70 times prewar.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: Coal-control bill delayed by Democratic refusal; bonuses for farmers delivering excess rice; 5 July civil-service reform demands; party statements by Liberals, Democrats, Cooperatives and Communists.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: House of Representatives held 143 Social Democrats among 466 seats; the Diet recessed 12-25 July; Seko alleged 50 billion yen in hidden war goods and a special committee was named.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: 569,400 persons screened since 4 January; Cabinet Order No. 119 (2 July) widened designation; Butoku-kai officials presumed purgeable; 41 media firms added to the blacklist.

sections.title: Personnel Changes and Local Government
sections.summary: Ashida was named deputy Prime Minister on 3 July; prefectural governors complained on 5 July that central branch offices violate local autonomy.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: May crime: 146,045 offenses and 69,893 arrests; June rail accidents killed 97; prison population 74,720; 1,361 fires; Tokyo adopted the azimuthal fire-spotting method.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: A 15-man committee recommended 30 Supreme Court candidates on 18 July; atrocity cases fell to 1,870; 286 defendants tried by 24 July, 276 convicted and 26 sentenced to death.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: June and July data for agriculture, mining, industry, utilities, communications, labor, trade, price control, finance and property control, mostly showing flat output limited by coal, power and materials shortages.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Land purchases reached 853,506 acres; religious-institution land made subject to reform; cool weather delayed northern crops; June fish catch fell 30,367 tons; 686 whales taken January-June.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: June logs 545,856,000 board feet; coal 2,128,000 tons with stockpiles at 738,800; crude oil 17,790 kiloliters with three new producers; 14 of 25 minerals gained in May.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke 153,500 tons; copper output cut by a mine strike; record 31,551 housing starts; 2,259,874 dwellings destroyed in major cities; chemical index 44 percent of requirements; 555 machine tools built.

sections.title: Coke, Metal Industries, Rubber, Petroleum and Cement
sections.summary: Pig iron up 6 percent and steel up 13 percent over May; aluminum fell to 871 tons; crude rubber imports 2,452 tons; 36 cement plants made 100,502 tons.

sections.title: Construction and Reconstruction of Bombed Cities
sections.summary: June building permits 33,229; second coal-miners' housing program (7,843 new, 14,645 repairs); 433,165 dwellings rebuilt in bombed cities against a shortage over 4,000,000.

sections.title: Shipbuilding and Chemical Industries
sections.summary: 438 vessels repaired in a month; calcium superphosphate 67,340 tons; cyanamide hit a postwar high of 24,903 tons; sulfuric acid fell to 122,755 tons for lack of pyrite.

sections.title: Machinery
sections.summary: Industrial machinery output 444.6 million yen; 13 steam locomotives and 95 passenger cars built; textile machinery value fell to 176 million yen as new units dropped 53 percent.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Canned food fell from 3,012 to 692 tons; paper output a record 29,900 tons; trucks 660, bicycles 16,028; sewing machines a postwar-high 6,689; toys 7,300,540 pieces.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: Cotton yarn peaked at 39,004,000 pounds; raw silk dropped to 9,171 bales; filament rayon hit 1,357,000 pounds; first wool cargo (7,481 bales) arrived from Australia in June.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Registered trucks and buses rose to 94,731 at 65.5-percent operation; 286,252,634 rail passengers; power generation 2,899,884,000 kWh, down 3 percent, with restrictions only in Chugoku and Kyushu.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: 9,773 new telephones installed; Ministry of Communications took over ship radio licensing (1,683 stations) on 15 July; mail volume fell after the 1 April rate rise; receiver tubes up 18 percent.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: Unions numbered 21,963 with 5,529,086 members; Transport Workers' Council formed 9 July; NCIU convention 10-14 July; standard wages released 5 July; coal wage rose 12 percent on 25 July.

sections.title: Labor Legislation and Employer/Labor Organizations
sections.summary: Labor Ministry Bill submitted; Coal Industry Reconstruction Council launched a six-point program 1 July; Kansai Economic Reconstruction Council opened 8 July; 600,000-member transport council formed.

sections.title: Labor Relations, Negotiations and Disputes
sections.summary: 110 unfair-practice charges since the Trade-union Law; Mitsubishi Heavy Industry agreed a 2,600-yen base for 50,000 workers; May disputes numbered 72 involving 107,110 workers; no major July stoppages.

sections.title: Labor Education, Wages and Employment
sections.summary: Kyoto Labor College opened 1 July with 135 students; standard wage schedule for 35 industries; 130 vocational counsellors assigned; 20,785 coal miners recruited in June.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Food imports fell 3 percent; cotton cloth shipped for the first time since the war to Argentina, Ceylon, Kenya and Turkey; first machinery shipment to the Ryukyus; 50 horses sent to Korea.

sections.title: Section 10. Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Price stabilization program with 65-times ceiling; staple deliveries up to 21.6 days late (Fukuoka); emergency 26-day July ration; 219,300 tons of imported food released; 90,088 violations in June.

sections.title: Price Stabilization and Food
sections.summary: Government stocks held 23.2 days of staple food on 30 June; farmers allowed 8-kilogram rice parcels to relatives; fresh fish 24,663 tons and vegetables 32,254 tons reached six cities.

sections.title: Producers' and Consumers' Goods; Violations and Controls
sections.summary: Fertilizer allotments linked to grain collections; crude oil raised to 3,451 yen per kiloliter; utility rates up one to four times; 582,077 price and ration violations January-June.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Six foreign banks licensed; Bank of Japan notes reached 143,745,746,371 yen on 31 July; 28 organizations closed in June; liquidation proceeds 2.92 billion yen; national debt 289,007,000,000 yen.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Neutral and Allied property totaled 909,648,000 yen; 299 looted ships reported; 2.1 billion yen authorized for rehabilitation, mostly coal; Fair Trade Commission seated 14 July; Indian reparations delegation arrived.

sections.title: Property Control
sections.summary: 1,580 reports processed in a month; property of 1,055 suspected war criminals in custody; SCAP held 257.5 million dollars in precious metals; yen custody account rose 40 million yen.

sections.title: Antitrust and Cartels; Reparations
sections.summary: 92 control companies closed; Mitsui and Mitsubishi Trading ordered dissolved; 56 Zaibatsu family members told to deliver securities; Antitrust Act fully effective 20 July; 32 machine-tool plants inspected.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare and repatriation figures, then education reforms, religion, cultural monuments and the month's information and media programs.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: 1,500,000 students dusted with DDT; 644 typhus cases typed; 3,363 hospitals; penicillin 355,560,000 units; welfare payments 285,248,000 yen; 65,672 repatriated; pensions raised 300 percent.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine and Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: Hokkaido typhus vaccination reached 638,857 full doses; Okayama encephalitis vaccine for 14,473; diphtheria, scarlet fever and smallpox fell below May; animal disease and meat inspection tables.

sections.title: Medical Supply, Narcotics and Public Assistance
sections.summary: Medical supplies 337,828,289 yen; 10-percent DDT dust 1,162,796 kg; 146 narcotics violators; new relief grant scale (10.80 yen daily for one person in large cities); LARA shipments arrived.

sections.title: Social Security, Repatriation and Vital Statistics
sections.summary: Compensation insurance moved to the Labor and Transportation ministries; 43,850 repatriated from Soviet areas; May births 201,070 against 94,232 deaths under new reporting procedures.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: First workshops for teachers of handicapped children (181 enrolled); 3.1 billion yen for lower secondary schools; chrysanthemum crest dropped from stamps; Kyoto cultural sites map; press, radio and film activity.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: University Accreditation Association formed 8 July; 62,309,327 textbooks authorized; correspondence courses planned; Chuo University won the first Emperor's Cup track meet.

sections.title: Religion, Arts and Monuments
sections.summary: Cabinet orders on state land used by shrines and temples; Fukuoka Village Shinto Directive conviction; 1,213 foreign missionaries; 1,066 National Treasure objects inspected.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: 42 opinion-survey agencies; land-reform kami-shibai campaign; Katayama's first broadcast to women; Saga newspaper convention 14-19 July; press criticism of Cabinet and Diet; film, theater and music notes.

sections.title: Map of Japan
sections.summary: Closing map of Japan, with a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers credit.
